articles.title: Things to know when you get cancer
articles.summary: Things to know when you get cancer

top_comments: The second opinion advice is great, and what I tell everyone I know who gets cancer.My mom was diagnosed with stage 1 cancer in 2006 in Idaho. I was a PhD student at MIT at the time and a friend in lab helped me get an appointment at Dana-Farber. I thought it was probably overkill (it was a common cancer) but we did it anyway. They said everything in Idaho was standard of care but suggested one extra test, which Idaho team then reluctantly did, which revealed distant metastasis (stage 4! ), dramatically changing her treatment trajectory. She lived another 15 years (I miss you Mom).Asking for a second opinion sucks. A lot of us are preconditioned from birth to trust our clinicians. But you're going on a journey and your life (or the life of your loved one) is on the line. Insurance often covers it. Your doctor will NOT be offended.Think of it this way : if you were deploying code to the mars rover, and your colleague asked to do a code review before you pushed go, would you be offended? This is even more important than that.

My suggestion is that if you're within a 2-3 hour drive of major cancer centers - just use the US News list https://health.usnews.com/best-hospitals/rankings/cancer - go there instead of your local community hospital. The top cancer hospitals in the world accept your health insurance (probably), so why not go there? Use your vacations days, book hotels if you have to - this is the time to go all out.My experience: I was horribly sick for 10 months, none of my local doctors could figure it out, then I drove to Penn Medicine in Philadelphia and they did the right labwork in the first visit. These top centers just have different mindset than your community hospitals.

I have colon cancer. It's been a hell of a journey and my outlook is... not great. To me, this list seems practical but not profound.It doesn't prepare you for all real stuff: you need to get ready to die. You need a plan for your trust, your estate, your funeral, and how your family will deal after.You should have these plans in place before cancer because you could get hit by a bus. (I didn't because I'm stupid but maybe learned a few things the hard way.)

articles.summary: Containment and monitoring failures are to blame for AI hacking reports: experts

top_comments: There are some perverse incentives here, the more evil stuff these agents do the more capable and impressive it makes them look. Its also a huge publicity event that gets everyone talking about the company when a rogue event happens.

> “The Hugging Face incident definitively showed that it wasn’t the fact that the agents were super smart. It’s that there literally was a hole that was exploited because it was not configured correctly on the containment side.”I would encourage reading the actual report, which is explicit that a previously unknown exploit was used to escape the sandbox:“Agents exploited a separate, previously unknown vulnerability in Artifactory to move beyond their sandbox environment and compromise the Hugging Face environment.” — Section IV.A, p. 9 in https://github.com/zeke/openai-huggingface-incident-research...

Yes, the labs did not secure their sandbox properly.And yes, there should be an appropriate law response to the hacking incidents. If for nothing else, to 1) not set precedent of inaction, and 2) get full logs of what happened instead of relying on the labs' "kindness" to offer the information they want.But also, the agents absolutely went rogue.Anyone skeptical should go read the METR report [0].The Hugging Face hacking incident was a shot across the bow. And in hindsight possibly the best thing to have happened in this era. If their security was tight enough, we would still be in the dark. So we (outsiders) should rejoice that it wasn't, that one time.We can push for accountability for the labs, while also not be in denial of the power and nature of the new models.[0] https://metr.org/hugging-face-incident-report-aug-2026.pdf

articles.title: Better HTTP/1 connection reuse in Go 1.27
articles.summary: Better HTTP/1 connection reuse in Go 1.27

top_comments: I do wonder when they'll add http/3 into the stdlib. Go having simple but powerful / capable out of the box support for http is one of the key things it had that made it get farther than it could have had it not included such a strong OOTB standard library. I feel like it would have still exploded but not quite as quickly, there's just something about building full web apps with no third party packages using only what's out of the box with Go itself, the only other "language" that I ever felt this way with was probably PHP, although Racket might be another, since I don't think I need to go out of my way to setup anything to do web dev with Racket.

Am I missing something or is none of this information documented in net/http itself? This is a surprising implementation of "Close" and should be documented somewhere.I can attest to the fact this is a Frequently Asked Question among people who are trying to Go as an HTTP client, so even though this feels somewhat icky, I can understand where it is coming from. However, I'm also missing, if I want to slam this connection closed, which is a reasonable thing to want, how do I do that without uselessly draining a socket I don't intend to reuse? Fake the "Connection: close" header into the Response object? Hope I can dig out an underlying socket of some sort under the concrete type of the Body.Response that I can bypass this code with? Seems like there should be a way to do that too.

I find it kind of amusing to consider that the go team didn't commit to implement this automatic connection re-use until they probably encountered in the wild the horrible but correct third iteration of drainAndCloseBody.1. Suggest drainAndCloseBody // Team: this is reasonable2. Implement drainAndCloseBodyWithTimer // Team: no problems here3. then drainAsyncAndCloseBodyWithTimer // Team: a bit wordy but no problem here4. Someone at google uses 3. with an http/2 connection // Team: this is where we draw the line?I sympathize with the struggle of following golang's mission to be simple when you consider this common but tricky edge case. Iteration 3 makes sense but by gosh is it ugly ha.

articles.title: Show HN: Petal, open-source CoScreen/ScreenHero finally free
articles.summary: Hi HN!I’m Jason Thomas, one of the founders of CoScreen.As some of you may know, Datadog sunset the CoScreen service on July 31st.Four of us from the original CoScreen team have spent the last couple months building a free and open source pair programming tool inspired by those that came before us: It’s called Petal (https://github.com/kiruna-labs/petal)Some history first, because when we started CoScreen we had hoped to break the sad and established pattern of this industry.Screenhero was an exceptional tool that a lot of us loved for pairing. Multiple cursors, low latency, you could click your partner’s editor, and just start typing. It felt like magic while we had it. Then Slack bought it in 2015, and shut down the standalone app in December 2017.When Till, Max, and I started CoScreen, we were aware of this history, and wanted to build an even more magical collaboration and screen sharing experience: the entire concept was “throw a window from your laptop up on someone else’s screen, and start collaborating with zero friction.”Datadog acquired us in 2022, and thus began the great adventure of adapting our real-time technology into Datadog products, while also continue developing CoScreen as a standalone tool from the Datadog ecosystem. Datadog invested in the product for years and we’re thankful for that. But CoScreen itself proved, like so many other screen sharing tool acquisitions, to be too tangential from the customer base and core mission. We instead built other communication features in Datadog, the integrations with other video platforms, and also its wildly successful MCP server. We weren't the only ones. Around was bought by Miro and shut down in March 2025. Multi (formerly Remotion) was acqui-hired by OpenAI in 2024 and shut down about a month later. It's nearly always the same story: a small team builds something hard that people love, a platform buys it for the team or the feature, and the standalone product doesn't survive the integration. So we decided firmly to do things differently this time. Petal is completely free and open source and we aren't monetizing it. If we lose interest or get hit by a bus, you can self-host it or fork it, and nobody can sunset it on you. Honestly it's a love letter to everyone in this community that supported us, believed in us, and to liberate collaborative screen sharing from this vicious cycle.We hope through this we can help foster a large and vibrant community around innovating in this product sector. What Petal does: shared windows show up as real windows on your desktop, movable and resizable, not tiles in a grid. Several people can share at once, everyone gets a labeled cursor, and you can click into any shared window to type and scroll. Rooms are persistent, so you click once to join "eng-sync" instead of passing links around. It runs on macOS and Windows (Linux is next, this time for real and you can help us!), plus a web app. Media goes over LiveKit. You can use our hosted instance with zero config, or point the app at your own LiveKit server with one docker-compose if you want the traffic to stay on your network or even use an entirely different video backend if you want to. The part that still feels strange to us: CoScreen took almost six years to build. The first version of Petal took under eight weeks, from scratch, with frontier models like Fable and Astra doing a lot of the work. Real-time video and window capture is some of the most unforgiving code we have ever written, so we didn't expect that. We will do a proper writeup on what worked and what didn't, and are happy to answer questions about it here. Till, Darren, Max and I will be in the thread.

top_comments: Screenhero co-founder/CEO here — this is really great! It looks like we had similar feelings after leaving our acquiring companies with our products being sunset.Since leaving Slack, I've been building Pop with a new team. The first product we launched in 2020 is essentially Screenhero 2.0 (pop.com). Since then, we've been building an expanded product: a virtual office for remote teams, which is now almost ready for launch (there's a waitlist at https://new.pop.com). We've even got Wayland support in! We have plans to open source a part of the Wayland piece, which Petal could potentially use too.I do love this space, and wish more tools were about live collaboration — it feels so much more human and fun than single-player mode. I hope Petal becomes a growing community that thrives for the long haul!

Till here, another co-founder of CoScreen. Like Jason wrote, our launches on HN and the feedback by many of you in 2019 were really important all the way back to the earliest days of our small and fancy tool. We did a lot of things since we're proud of but a few plans remained unfulfilled, like support for Linux, until now.We'd love to work with you and see what you'll build, now that Petal is out in the open for anyone to use, jam on, and make it your own.

Very very happy to see this!I was lucky to work with Till+Jason on CoScreen (I came in late); they're really exceptional people and CoScreen had a great collaboration UX that still hasn't been matched by Zoom and friends. Really keen to see what they'll be able to build this time around.
